title: What do the letters mean?
told: a sakhi from the Janamsakhis, a traditional story

hook.say: a question first. when did you last ask, “but what does it mean?”
options: then you already have the gift. listen.

steps.line: When Nanak was about seven, his father took him to the village teacher, the pandha, to learn his letters and one day keep accounts like his dad.
steps.label: a traditional sakhi

steps.line: The teacher wrote the alphabet on a wooden board, a patti, and told the boy to copy it. Nanak did.

steps.q: Nanak copies the letters, then asks the teacher what they really mean, what they point to. How does the teacher respond?
steps.why: The village teacher is stumped. And the seven-year-old starts to explain.

steps.line: Then he asked: but what do they mean? Not what sound they make. What do they point to? The teacher had no answer.
So the boy began to explain. Each letter could point toward God. The first, toward the One who made everything. The next, toward truth. And on and on.

steps.q: The letters Nanak learned grew into the script Sikhs use today, Gurmukhi. Which Guru does tradition say shaped it?
o: Guru Nanak himself, as a boy
steps.why: Tradition credits Guru Angad with shaping Gurmukhi, “from the Guru’s mouth,” so ordinary people could read the hymns themselves.

steps.line: In the story, the teacher bowed to his student.
The scripture really holds a poem by Guru Nanak called Patti, the writing board. Each letter opens a line about God. Some think he wrote it grown up.

steps.q: Patti’s refrain says you’re truly educated only when something happens. When?
o: When you can read every letter
When your life’s account is settled
When a teacher signs your board
steps.why: “When you give your account, brother, then you are educated.” A neat turn for a boy sent to school to learn bookkeeping.

steps.q: The word “Sikh” itself comes from an old word. What does it mean?
steps.why: Sikh means a learner, a student of the Guru. Fitting, for a faith whose founder’s story starts at school with a question.

say: here’s what i love. guru nanak wasn’t against learning. tradition says he later studied persian with a muslim teacher, and sanskrit too.

he just wouldn’t stop at the surface. the same question runs under his whole life: what does this really point to? many sikhs read gurbani, the gurus’ words, that way. not only reciting, but asking what it means.

steps.q: Patti walks through the alphabet on a writing board. If he wrote it grown up, why might the tellers set it on his first school day?
o: Old school records dated it to then
He said himself he wrote it at seven
An ABC poem fits a first school day
steps.why: Many scholars think sakhis like this grew out of the hymns: an alphabet poem on a writing board found its home in a schoolroom. Its question fits any age.

today.say: today, take one word you use every day, home, sorry, friend, and ask nanak’s question of it: what does this really point to? let it open slowly.
options: good choice. see where it points.
even better. it’s yours to ask.

tomorrow.line: a boy falls asleep in the fields. something comes out of the grass.

sources: Janamsakhi traditions of Nanak at the pandha’s school (the teacher is named Gopal in some tellings)
Patti, Raag Asa, Guru Nanak, Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 432 (an acrostic; its first letter, sassa, names the One who made the world, and the next, eevri, the True One); not quoted, only described
Tradition of Nanak studying Persian with a Muslim teacher
check: Persian and Sanskrit study are tradition (teachers often named as Qutb-ud-din and Brij Nath).
